find: In the Edexcel Component 2, Section A question, you will be given a short extract and asked two parts: Part (a) asks you to analyse language closely in the extract (AO1 + AO2), and Part (b) asks you to explore the wider text.
replace: In the Edexcel 19th-century novel question you get a printed extract and answer two parts. Part (a) is worth 20 marks and rewards close analysis of Dickens’s language and structure (AO2, the writer’s methods). Part (b) is worth 20 marks and rewards your own argument about the whole novella, backed by quotations (AO1, your response).
note: F2: part (a) is AO2 only and part (b) is AO1 only on this section; the old text also used a banned section code.

find: This approach earns AO1 marks by linking context to the writer’s purpose.
replace: Context itself earns no marks on this question, so keep it short and use it only to sharpen a point about Dickens’s purpose.
note: F2: AO3 (context) is not assessed on the 19th-century novel section.

find: Dickens opens the novella with a bold, conversational declaration: “Old Marley was as dead as a doornail.”
replace: Dickens opens the novella with a blunt statement of fact: “Marley was dead: to begin with.” A few lines later the narrator turns it into the famous simile: “Old Marley was as dead as a doornail.”
note: F3: the first line is "Marley was dead: to begin with." The door-nail simile comes five sentences later.
F3: the key marked the true first line wrong. Option 1 is "Marley was dead: to begin with."

find: The repetition of the same consonant sound at the beginning of nearby words, used for emphasis and rhythm.
replace: The repetition of 's' sounds, often creating a hissing, cold or sinister quality.
note: F4: that was the definition of alliteration, not sibilance. The glossary already has it right.

find: Marley tells Scrooge that his own chain was “as heavy and as long as this” seven years ago, and has grown since.
replace: Marley tells Scrooge that Scrooge’s own chain was “full as heavy and as long as this, seven Christmas Eves ago,” and that he has laboured on it since.
note: F5: the Ghost says this of the coil Scrooge already bears, not of Marley's chain.

find: the fog is “cold, bleak, biting,” and the weather is so severe that the city is wrapped in darkness
replace: the weather is “cold, bleak, biting,” and the fog is so thick that the city is wrapped in darkness
note: F6: Dickens writes "It was cold, bleak, biting weather"; the phrase describes the weather, not the fog.

find: streamed from beneath it, in an unbroken flood upon the ground.
replace: streamed from under it, in an unbroken flood upon the ground.
note: F8: the text reads "which streamed from under it".
F9: Belle says "Another idol has displaced me" and "A golden one." "Golden idol" is not in the novella.

find: “If these shadows remain unaltered by the Future, I see a vacant chair … and a crutch without an owner.”
replace: “I see a vacant seat … and a crutch without an owner, carefully preserved. If these shadows remain unaltered by the Future, the child will die.”
note: F10: the text reads "vacant seat", and the conditional follows the image rather than opening it.

find: The image of the empty chair and the abandoned crutch is deeply affecting.
replace: The image of the empty seat and the abandoned crutch is deeply affecting.
note: F10: follows the corrected quotation.

expect: 'A vacant chair... and a crutch without an owner.'
value: 'A vacant seat... and a crutch without an owner.'
note: F10: same correction on the memorisation card.

find: A comparison between two things without using 'like' or 'as'. The spirit moving 'like a mist' technically uses 'like', making it a simile, but the overall presentation of the ghost as Death itself functions as extended metaphor.
replace: A comparison between two things using 'like' or 'as'. The ghost moves 'like a mist', while its overall presentation as Death itself works as an extended metaphor.
note: F11: the tooltip for "simile" gave the definition of metaphor.

find: This <dfn class="term" data-def="A technique where the audience or reader knows something that a character does not, or where information is withheld to build tension.">dramatic irony</dfn> is devastatingly effective.
replace: This is suspense rather than <dfn class="term" data-def="A technique where the reader knows something that a character does not.">dramatic irony</dfn>, and it is devastatingly effective: the reader is kept in the dark alongside Scrooge until the gravestone.
note: F12: the reader knows no more than Scrooge here, and the definition had been widened until it no longer described dramatic irony.

Level 2–3 (5–9 marks): Some valid comments about language with limited analysis of effects.
Lower band (1-4): Simple identification of features with minimal comment.

Level 4–5 (10–16 marks): Clear analysis with relevant contextual links.
Level 2–3 (5–9 marks): Some valid points about Scrooge’s attitude with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-4): Simple comments about Scrooge being mean.

Level 2–3 (5–9 marks): Some relevant points with limited development.
